title: What if you sank into the deepest blue hole?

hook.banner: How deep is the deepest blue hole?

narration.heading: The drop
narration.text: You're swimming in a bay just five metres deep. Then the floor simply drops away.

narration.heading: Taam Ja'
narration.text: This is Taam Ja', in Chetumal Bay, Mexico. A local diver found it around 2003, following a grouper inside.

narration.heading: The funnel
narration.text: Its walls plunge almost straight down, steeper than eighty degrees, like a giant funnel.

narration.heading: No oxygen
narration.text: Twenty metres down, oxygen is already low. Past a hundred and ten, there's none at all.

narration.heading: First guess
narration.text: Scientists first measured it at two hundred and seventy-four metres. The second-deepest blue hole known.

narration.heading: Still going
narration.text: But in December 2023, a probe on a cable kept going. Past three hundred. Past four hundred.

narration.heading: 420 m down
narration.text: It stopped at over four hundred and twenty metres. Now it's the deepest blue hole known.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? Its deepest water matches the Caribbean Sea. It may be secretly linked to the ocean by caves.

narration.heading: Bottomless?
narration.text: And still, nobody has found the bottom. How deep do you think it goes?

skit.text: No bottom found? Same as my search history.

titles: What if you sank into the deepest blue hole on Earth?
Taam Ja': the blue hole with no bottom found yet
youtube.description: Sink into Taam Ja', a blue hole in Mexico's Chetumal Bay, through water with no oxygen, past 420 metres, and find out why it may be secretly connected to the Caribbean Sea.

sources.claim: Taam Ja' Blue Hole is in Chetumal Bay, Mexico, and was discovered around 2003 by a local diver following a grouper; it is the deepest known blue hole

Taam Ja' sits in Chetumal Bay at about 5 m depth, with slopes steeper than 80°; it has a hypoxic layer at 5–20 m, a chemocline at 50–80 m and anoxic water below about 110 m; first measured at 274.4 m, then described as the second-deepest known blue hole

CTD casts on 6 and 13 December 2023 reached 423.6 m without reaching the bottom; deep water below 400 m resembles Caribbean seawater, suggesting a possible subterranean connection; temperature layers from about 27 °C at the surface to 19.8 °C at 332–399 m
Dragon Hole in the South China Sea is about 301 m deep and was the deepest known blue hole until Taam Ja' surpassed it in 2024
